taxonomyNote: NatureServe and the SSAR list (Nicholson 2025) recognise a single species, the Rubber Boa, with northern (C. b. bottae) and southern (C. b. umbratica) subspecies; earlier authors (Crother 2017) treated the southern form as a separate species.
fieldMarks: Usually 38-64 cm (range 35-84 cm); thick, smooth-scaled body with loose, wrinkled skin that looks and feels like rubber.
Uniform brown to olive-green above and yellow to cream below; occasional dark spots or mottling (more often in northern populations).
Small dark eyes with vertical pupils.
Blunt, head-like tail tip with a bulb of bone, usually scarred; the snake curls up and presents the tail when threatened.
Northern subspecies has sub-triangular frontal scales and 42 or more mid-dorsal scale rows; the southern subspecies has fewer.
behavior: Solitary, burrowing and slow-moving; mostly nocturnal or at dusk, but also active by day in mild cloudy weather, and sometimes basks.
Active mostly March-November; docile, does not strike, and deters predators with the tail or a strong odour.
Eats nestling mice, voles and shrews found in nests, and occasionally lizard or snake eggs; found under rotting logs, stumps, rocks and bark.
Prehensile tail allows it to climb shrubs and small trees.
habitat: Moist coniferous forest, woodlands, forest clearings, meadows and grassy streamsides, generally not far from water, from sea level to about 3,050 m.
Uses rodent burrows, rock outcrops, fallen logs and deep duff for cover.
range: Southern British Columbia and Alberta south to west-central California, central Nevada and southern Utah; Pacific coast east to north-central Wyoming and western Montana. Distribution is patchy, especially at southern and eastern edges.
